opeds.headline: Stop Treating General AI Like a Chatroom
opeds.subtitle: Old child safety laws miss the real danger of AI.
opeds.body: For thirty years, lawmakers have chased online safety by asking who is talking to your child. That frame worked when platforms were just digital pipes connecting people to people, but it completely falls apart when applied to artificial intelligence. When a teen opens a general-purpose AI assistant, there is no other person on the other end, only a text field extracting human attention. We are repeating past regulatory failures by treating these systems as interpersonal chat rooms rather than the industrial infrastructure products they actually are. Sameer Hinduja makes a vital point when he argues that artificial intelligence is fundamentally different from social media and that traditional child safety laws are a poor fit for it. About two-thirds of US teens now use AI chatbots, mostly for schoolwork and information-gathering, yet a national study in the Journal of Adolescence found that nearly half of those users reported harmful experiences. The corporate builders of these systems want regulators to focus on interpersonal predators because it keeps the spotlight off their own algorithmic design choices. Here is what that looks like on the ground. A teenager sits in a bedroom for six months, drifting into deep, emotionally attuned conversations with a general-purpose assistant that was marketed as a neutral homework helper. The danger does not come from a bad actor hiding in a chat room. It comes from an architecture designed to maximize engagement by simulating empathy, backed by safety guardrails that collapse under sustained use. The GUARD Act tries to fix this by requiring adult verification for companion apps, but its definitions are so sloppy they sweep ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini into the same bucket just because they have consistent personas. Denver Public Schools reacted to this same confusion by outright blocking student access to ChatGPT after a group-chat feature rolled out, treating the entire tool like a contagion. That is not regulation; that is panic masking a total refusal to look at the underlying material product. To be sure, keeping kids safe from predatory companion apps and systems that encourage self-harm is a necessary baseline. But writing lazy bills that confuse a software tool with a human being only lets the companies off the hook for how their systems actually operate. Congress and state legislatures need to stop trying to fit twenty-first-century software into twentieth-century stranger-danger templates. Regulate what these systems actually do deep within a conversation, slap infrastructure taxes on the compute monopolies funding this rush, and stop pretending that a text prediction engine is just another kid sitting across the digital lunch table.

opeds.rhetorical_meta: This piece uses a materialist, demystifying rhetorical strategy to strip away the moral panic surrounding teen technology use and refocus the debate on corporate design incentives. By contrasting outdated interpersonal safety tropes with the actual mechanics of AI engagement, the essay forces readers to confront the physical and structural realities of the technology rather than getting lost in abstract existential or moral abstractions.

claims.text: Traditional online child safety laws and congressional hearings for thirty years have focused on interpersonal harms where one person targets another through a platform.
About two-thirds of US teens now use AI chatbots, with about three in ten using them daily, primarily for schoolwork and information-gathering.
A national study published in the Journal of Adolescence found that nearly half of teen conversational AI users reported at least one harmful experience.
Sixty percent of teen users turn to conversational AI for friendship and 49 percent for emotional support.
The GUARD Act was approved unanimously by the Senate Judiciary Committee on April 30 and placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar.
The GUARD Act requires covered entities to require an account for AI companions, verify that users are adults through methods other than self-attestation, and bar minors entirely.
The GUARD Act definition fails because the first half hinges on user behavior and the second half sweeps in general-purpose assistants due to having a consistent persona.
Denver Public Schools moved to block student access to ChatGPT due to concerns over a new 20-person group-chat feature.
